body:
Understanding costume traditions

Traditional Indian clothing includes draped garments, stitched garments, headgear, shawls and ornaments. Clothing provides protection from the environment while expressing regional customs, occupation, religious identity and social occasions.

A useful distinction is between the form of a garment, the material from which it is made and the decorative method used to produce it.

A sari is a garment, silk is a textile fibre, and ikat is a method of creating patterned textiles. A silk Patan Patola sari combines all 3 characteristics.

Draped and stitched garments

Draped garments

Draped garments consist primarily of cloth arranged around the body without the main fabric being permanently stitched into a fitted shape.

  • Sari: A long cloth worn around the lower body, with an end portion called the pallu arranged over the upper body.
  • Dhoti: A cloth wrapped around the waist and lower body, traditionally worn by men in many regions.
  • Mundu: A lower-body garment traditionally associated with Kerala.
  • Lungi: A cloth worn around the waist, commonly used in several southern, eastern and northeastern regions.
  • Pagri or turban: Cloth arranged around the head, with considerable variation in regional styles.

These garments are not restricted to a single type of fabric. A sari, for example, may be made from cotton, silk or synthetic materials.

Stitched garments

Stitched garments are formed by sewing pieces of fabric into a particular shape. Examples include the kurta, salwar, kameez, choli, ghagra and pheran.

A salwar kameez consists of trousers and an upper garment, often accompanied by a dupatta. A ghagra choli consists of a skirt and fitted upper garment, commonly accompanied by an odhni or dupatta.

Important regional costumes

RegionTraditional attireIdentifying feature
KashmirPheranLoose, long outer garment
Himachal PradeshRegional caps and shawlsHeadgear and protection against cold
PunjabSalwar kameez and Patiala salwarLoose trousers with upper garment
RajasthanGhagra, choli, odhni and pagriSkirt, blouse, veil and regional headgear
GujaratChaniya choli, kediyu and chornoDistinctive western Indian costume forms
MaharashtraNauvari sariTraditional 9-yard sari
KeralaMundu and mundum neriyathumLower-body cloth and traditional 2-piece women's attire
AssamMekhela chadorLower wrap and upper draped cloth
NagalandTraditional woven shawlsCommunity-specific patterns
MizoramPuan and puancheiTraditional woven cloth and festive attire

Clothing and ecology

The pheran of Kashmir illustrates adaptation to cold weather. Its loose outer form provides space for layered clothing, and warmer fabrics are used during winter.

In hot regions, lightweight cotton garments and loose clothing are often preferred. Draped garments permit considerable variation in fit and use. Turbans may protect the head from sunlight while also expressing community and ceremonial identity.

However, colourful or elaborate clothing in arid regions cannot be explained by climate alone. Aesthetic preferences, inherited customs and social meanings are equally important.

The sari as an example of unity in diversity

The sari is a widespread Indian garment, but its regional forms differ in fabric, length, weaving, motifs, borders and draping styles.

A stone relief from Vaishali in present-day Bihar depicts an ancient sari-like draped garment and provides evidence of the long history of this clothing form.

The Maharashtrian nauvari sari, the Gujarati front-facing pallu drape and various eastern and southern draping traditions illustrate regional variation within a shared garment form.

Dress and social identity

Traditional clothing may communicate community membership, marital status, ceremonial roles and occupation. Northeast Indian shawls, for example, can carry patterns associated with particular communities, while western Indian embroidery may distinguish community-specific traditions.

Such associations are customary rather than universal. Modern clothing choices, migration and changing occupations have made many formerly distinctive garments widely available.

Prelims focus

  • Pheran is a traditional loose outer garment associated with Kashmir.
  • Nauvari is the traditional 9-yard sari associated with Maharashtra.
  • Mekhela is the lower garment and chador is the upper draped cloth in Assamese attire.
  • Mundu is associated with Kerala.
  • Puan and puanchei are associated with Mizoram.
  • Trap: A garment form such as a sari is not the same as its fibre or weaving technique.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 8, Textiles and Clothing, pp. 128–131; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, regional Dress sections; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Crafts Heritage, pp. 9–10; Kerala Tourism, traditional dress of Kerala; Barpeta District Administration, traditional Assamese attire. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Traditional Indian Clothing: Garment Forms, Climate and Identity

body:
Major textile fibres

The properties and availability of textile fibres influence the production and use of traditional clothing. Cotton, silk and wool have particularly important roles in Indian textile heritage.

FibreSourceTraditional use
CottonCotton plantEveryday garments and lightweight textiles
SilkCocoons of silk-producing insectsSaris, ceremonial garments and shawls
WoolAnimal fleece or hairWarm garments, blankets and shawls
PashminaFine underfleece of Himalayan goatsFine shawls and other warm textiles

India has several silk traditions. Mulberry silk is used extensively in silk weaving, while muga, eri and tasar represent important non-mulberry silk traditions.

Muga silk, especially associated with Assam, is known for its natural golden appearance. Eri silk is important in Assam and other northeastern regions, while tasar silk traditions are prominent in parts of eastern and central India.

Basic textile methods

Traditional textiles can acquire their patterns at different stages of production. Understanding the stage at which a pattern is created helps distinguish weaving, dyeing, printing and embroidery.

Weaving

Weaving produces fabric by interlacing 2 sets of threads. The warp consists of lengthwise threads, while the weft passes across them.

In patterned weaving, decorative designs become part of the fabric as it is woven.

Ikat

Ikat is a resist-dyeing method in which selected portions of yarn are protected from dye before the yarn is woven. The arranged dyed threads produce the desired pattern in the finished cloth.

Tie-dye and printing

In fabric tie-dye, selected portions of an existing cloth are tied to prevent dye penetration. Bandhani is an important Indian example.

Block printing produces designs by applying colour or printing substances to cloth using carved blocks.

Embroidery and metallic decoration

Embroidery decorates existing fabric using a needle and thread. Mirrors, beads and other decorative materials may also be attached to the cloth.

Zari is a metallic decorative thread traditionally associated with gold and silver. Brocade is a richly patterned woven fabric that may incorporate zari or other decorative threads.

Important embroidery and surface-decoration traditions

TraditionRegionBasic feature
PhulkariPunjabColourful embroidery, often featuring floral motifs
ChikankariLucknow, Uttar PradeshFine embroidery on fabric

Sujini or SujniBiharEmbroidery associated with decorative and narrative designs
KasutiKarnatakaTraditional counted-thread embroidery
Toda embroideryNilgiri Hills, Tamil NaduRed and black embroidery on a light-coloured base
Kutchi embroideryGujaratCommunity-specific embroidery and mirror-work traditions

The distinctive embroidered shawl of the Toda community is known by transliterated names including Puthukkuli and Pootkhull. Despite its woven-looking patterns, the decoration is created through needlework.

Uppada Jamdani is a weaving tradition of Andhra Pradesh. Sujini is an embroidery tradition of Bihar, and Toda embroidery belongs to the Nilgiri Hills of Tamil Nadu. These are distinct textile forms.

Historical significance of Indian textiles

Indian cotton textiles were traded across Asia and Europe. Chintz, a patterned cotton textile, became especially popular in 17th-century Europe. Its popularity led England and France to introduce restrictions on Indian printed cotton imports and use in order to protect their domestic textile industries.

Textile traditions therefore reflect not only local clothing requirements but also India's historical involvement in long-distance trade and cultural exchange.

Prelims focus

  • Muga is a silk tradition associated especially with Assam; pashmina is an animal-derived fine wool fibre.
  • Ikat creates patterns through resist-dyeing yarn before weaving.
  • Phulkari is associated with Punjab, Chikankari with Lucknow and Sujini with Bihar.
  • Toda embroidery is associated with the Nilgiris of Tamil Nadu.
  • Uppada Jamdani is associated with Andhra Pradesh.
  • Trap: Pochampally Ikat and Gadwal saris are associated with Telangana, not present-day Andhra Pradesh.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Crafts Heritage, pp. 9–12; NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 8, pp. 128–130; Ministry of Textiles, A Compendium of Indian Handicrafts and Handlooms Covered under Geographical Indications, 2017, regional textile entries and pp. 144, 155 and 157; Press Information Bureau, The Magic of Indian Silk, 11 April 2025; Press Information Bureau and Ministry of Textiles, Threads That Bind India: A Regional Glimpse of Timeless Traditions, 6 August 2025; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, regional Handicrafts sections. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Indian Textile Materials, Decorative Methods and Regional Traditions

body:
Traditional women's clothing

Gujarati women's clothing includes saris, chaniya cholis, ghagra cholis and various community-specific garments. Colours, fabrics, embroidery and ornaments vary between regions, communities and occasions.

Chaniya choli

The traditional chaniya choli consists of a flared skirt called the chaniya and an upper garment called the choli. It is commonly accompanied by an odhni or dupatta.

The outfit is especially associated with festive occasions such as Navratri. Embroidery, mirror work, colourful fabrics and decorative borders contribute to its distinctive appearance.

Gujarati sari drape

In a characteristic Gujarati draping style, the pallu is brought over the shoulder and arranged across the front of the body. This makes the decorative end portion of the sari prominently visible.

Other sari draping styles are also worn throughout Gujarat. The front-facing pallu is an important traditional association rather than a compulsory regional practice.

Traditional men's clothing

GarmentDescription
KediyuTraditional upper garment, commonly featuring pleats or flared construction
Chorno or choranuLoose traditional lower garment
DhotiUnstitched lower-body cloth
KurtaStitched upper garment
Phento or pagdiTraditional headgear or turban

The combination of kediyu, chorno and colourful headgear is associated particularly with traditional rural and festive dress. Contemporary festival costumes may combine the kediyu with other lower garments.

Regional and community variations

Kutch and Saurashtra

Kutch and Saurashtra contain numerous pastoral, agricultural and artisan communities with distinctive costume traditions. Rabari, Ahir, Bharwad, Jat and other communities have historically developed particular garment forms, embroidery styles and ornaments.

Rabari and Ahir embroidery traditions are especially associated with decorative threadwork and mirrors. The Banni region of Kutch is known for the diverse embroidery traditions of its communities, including Jat, Mutwa and Meghwal artisans.

Garment colours, embroidery motifs and the shape of an upper garment have historically helped communicate community affiliation and, in some contexts, marital status.

Tribal communities of eastern Gujarat

The tribal communities of eastern Gujarat possess distinct clothing and ornament traditions. Their dress has been shaped by agricultural livelihoods, inherited customs and local material resources.

Traditional Dangi women's clothing includes a cotton sari arranged in a regional draping style known as kachhota. Historical Dangi men's clothing included loincloths, dhotis and a short tunic or waistcoat-like garment called bandy. Modern clothing is also widely adopted.

Gujarati bridal textiles

Panetar

Panetar is a traditional Gujarati bridal sari, characteristically having a white or cream body with a red or maroon border and pallu.

In many Gujarati Hindu and Jain wedding traditions, the panetar is presented by the bride's maternal family, often through her maternal uncle.

Gharchola

Gharchola, also known as gharcholu, is a traditional ceremonial bridal textile, commonly characterised by a red or maroon base and a grid-like design. Its grid may incorporate zari work and Bandhani motifs.

It is traditionally associated with a gift from the groom's family and with the bride's entry into her married household.

Both are important Gujarati wedding textiles. Their exact colours, fabrics, gifting customs and manner of wearing vary among families and communities.

Patola in ceremonial clothing

Silk Patola is highly valued for auspicious and ceremonial use. It may be worn by brides, married women or family members according to local wedding customs.

Patola differs from Panetar and Gharchola because its name primarily identifies a textile-weaving tradition, while the latter names identify particular ceremonial textiles.

Ornaments and identity

Silver ornaments, bangles, anklets, necklaces, nose ornaments, earrings and beadwork form part of several Gujarati costume traditions. Silver jewellery is particularly associated with many rural, pastoral and tribal communities.

Ornaments and textiles may indicate ceremonial roles or inherited community customs. Their use changes with economic circumstances, fashion, migration and personal preferences.

Prelims focus

  • Chaniya is the skirt, choli is the upper garment and odhni is the covering cloth.
  • Kediyu is an upper garment; chorno is a lower garment.
  • Panetar commonly has a white or cream body with a red border.
  • Gharchola is characterised by a ceremonial grid pattern, often incorporating Bandhani and zari.
  • Banni in Kutch is associated with diverse community embroidery traditions.
  • Trap: Panetar, Gharchola and Patola are not interchangeable names for the same textile tradition.

[References: GSSTB, Standard 10, Social Science, Chapter 2, Cultural Heritage of India: Traditional Handicraft and Fine Arts, pp. 8–10, accessible online chapter extract; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, first edition, 2018, Gujarat, Dress section; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Crafts Heritage, pp. 9–10; Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook: The Dangs, Part A, Major Characteristics of the District; District Administration, Kachchh, Handicraft, Bandhani section; Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya, 15 Variations on the Sari, Gharcholu and Patola Sari entries; Gaatha, Bandhani Kutch, traditional bridal textiles section. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
